 Follow Country and bluegrass legend dies in his sleep at 95: ‘The music world lost a pioneer’
 Brian Linder Fri, November 6, 2026 at 10:01 AM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Bill Clifton might not be a name that every modern country music and bluegrass fan knows, but his significance cannot be denied.
 And that is because Clifton was not just a talented singer and musician; he was also an important figure in the preservation and promotion of Appalachian music.
 Sadly, Clifton, whose real name was William August Marburg, died on Oct. 30.
 He was 95.
 Bluegrass Today reported that Clifton died in his sleep.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "He devoted his life to ensuring that the traditional American music he loved would continue to be heard by future generations," his obituary read. "A musician, collector, publisher, festival organizer, and international ambassador for bluegrass, he carried the old songs to audiences across the United States and the world."
 Clifton grew up on a farm just outside of Baltimore and discovered country music while listening to the radio. That sparked a passion that resulted in nearly 30 albums. He released his first, "Mountain Folk Songs," on Starday records in 1960. His last, "Mountain Laurel," was released in 2004.
 Clifton's obituary said that he formed his first group, The Dixie Mountain Boys, while he was a student at the University of Virginia.
 His talent and impact were not limited to his voice and his ability to play an instrument, though.
 Advertisement Advertisement Clifton served in the Marines for two years after graduating from Virginia, and it was during that time that he put together his book, "Bill Clifton 150 Old-Time Folk and Gospel Songs."
 "The songbook became a valued resource for bluegrass musicians and later formed part of the preservation legacy recognized by his induction into the Bluegrass Music Hall of Fame," his obituary read.
 Clifton also organized one of the first bluegrass festivals in the country in 1961 in Luray, Virginia.
 He didn't stop there.
 Clifton packed up and moved his family to England, where he was credited with introducing a new audience to bluegrass. Later in life, as a member of the Peace Corps, he did the same in the Philippines.
 Advertisement Advertisement "Looking back on his career, Bill often said he was proudest of representing musicians who did not have the opportunity to bring their music to audiences beyond where they lived," his obituary read. "Whether introducing bluegrass overseas, arranging performances for traditional musicians, or bringing old songs to new listeners, he believed his greatest contribution was helping others and their music be heard."
 Musician and DJ Chris Jones called Cligton "a musical pioneer and someone who bridged bluegrass, folk and old time country music in a way that wasn't being done at the time."
 "The music world lost a pioneer today," musician Dennis Cash wrote on Facebook. "I lost a hero."
 The Bluegrass Music Hall of Fame & Museum issued a statement following his death.
 Advertisement Advertisement "Bill Clifton's legacy is one of passion, preservation, and a lifelong commitment to ensuring that traditional American music would continue to be heard and appreciated by future generations," it read. "His contributions helped carry bluegrass music across generations around the world."
